description: We are SpaceDAO, a team from Florianópolis, Brazil. Dayon (product, UX, vision) shaped the game and its story. Charlie (mission engine, council, cryptography, deploy) built the simulation that flies every design and the quantum-safe signatures. Eric (3D, flight, open-tech network) built the 3D Earth, Moon and launch. We believe space belongs to humanity, and that the next great mission will be designed by many nations at one table.
summary: SpaceDAO is a web game where players design, manage and simulate a complete space mission and see how every engineering choice shapes its success. You represent a space agency or company, choose three partners for a four-member council, and design one of three real missions: a lab on the space station, a satellite that watches fires and floods, or a base at the Moon's south pole. Every choice of rocket, orbit and module moves six live gauges: mass, power, budget, data, comms and lifetime. Partners review the design like a NASA Go / No-Go poll, with real numbers: one NO-GO holds the launch, and a unanimous GO opens a 4-of-4 post-quantum signature (NIST FIPS 204). Then you fly into real solar storms from NASA records, run the mission turn by turn, and the Debrief explains why it worked or failed. Why it matters: in space, the hardest part is often not the engineering but getting many nations to agree, pay and fly together. SpaceDAO runs the council as a DAO (Decentralized Autonomous Organization: a group that shares a budget and decides by rules everyone can read, with every vote on public record). It is our proposal for how nations could share technology, rockets and data. Free in the browser: no wallet, no tokens, no money.
details:
THE IDEA IN ONE MINUTE


The Outer Space Treaty (1967) says the exploration and use of outer space "shall be the province of all mankind". In practice, space is already a team sport: five agencies from fifteen nations run the International Space Station together. But every partnership is still negotiated one treaty at a time. Designs stay behind export rules, data sits in separate archives, and most of the world watches from outside.


At the same time, the internet has produced a new way to organize people across borders: groups that pool money, vote and act together under rules written in code. SpaceDAO connects the two. It is a mission design game, and it is also our proposal for a planetary space organization: one shared mission table where agencies, companies, scientists and funders decide together, share technology and spare rocket capacity, and bring the science back open to everyone.


FOUR WORDS YOU NEED (NO CRYPTO BACKGROUND REQUIRED)

- DAO (Decentralized Autonomous Organization): a group that shares a treasury and makes decisions by rules everyone can read. Votes and payments are recorded on a public ledger, so no single member can quietly change the outcome. Think of a cooperative whose bylaws run as software. In the game: your four-member council is a small DAO. Nothing launches without every partner's vote.

- Smart contract and multi-signature: a program that holds the rules of an agreement and executes them by itself. A "4-of-4 multi-signature" means four independent keys must sign before an action happens, the same way a launch needs every station to say GO. In the game: the mission manifest is signed by all four partners, and the game verifies each signature.

- Post-quantum signature: a digital signature designed to stay unforgeable even against future quantum computers. NIST published the standard in 2024 (FIPS 204, ML-DSA). Space programs and treaties last decades, so a signature made today must still be trusted in 2050. In the game: every signature is real, made in your browser with ed25519 plus ML-DSA-65.

- Network state: an online community that organizes, funds and governs itself across borders before it has any territory. Space has no borders by treaty, so it is a natural place for this idea. In the game: the SpaceDAO network, where each design you publish becomes an open blueprint others can adopt.


WHY THIS MATTERS NOW

- The space economy is growing fast: the World Economic Forum and McKinsey (2024) project it to reach 1.8 trillion US dollars by 2035. More missions will be flown by coalitions of agencies, companies and universities, and they need fair, transparent ways to decide and share.

- Internet communities have already shown they can fund and govern big goals together: ConstitutionDAO gathered about 47 million US dollars from thousands of people in under a week (2021), and MoonDAO, a community run as a DAO, has sent members to space on suborbital flights.

- Web3 kept growing while the world's attention moved to AI. Decentralized finance, DAOs and network-state projects keep attracting builders and major tech investors. Quadratic funding, a method where many small contributions count more than a few large ones, already funds open-source software. These tools let people anywhere fund and govern shared work across borders and currencies, without a company contract in every country.

- The technology is already moving to orbit: satellites broadcast public ledgers from space, and cryptographic hardware is being tested in orbit.

- What is missing is a place where students, scientists and the public can try this way of working on a real mission and see its trade-offs. That is SpaceDAO.

WHAT IT DOES

The player moves through seven steps, shown in a journey bar:

1. Mission: pick one of three real missions. Orbital Lab (easy): 30 days of science on the space station. Earth Guardian (medium): a satellite that watches fires, floods and farms, with downlink to ground stations in the Global South. Moon Base Zero (hard): the first outpost at the lunar south pole, with water ice, the long night and no direct view of Earth.

2. Team: represent a space agency or company and choose three partners for your council, from 18 space agencies and 16 companies.

3. Design: set the mission charter, objectives, rocket, orbit and spacecraft modules. Six gauges (mass, power, budget, data, comms, lifetime) react to every choice. Adopt open designs other teams shared, and rent your rocket's spare room to another team's experiment to earn budget.

4. Review and Sign: a Go / No-Go readiness review. Each partner owns the engineering checks that fit its strengths and votes GO, GO IF (with a condition) or NO-GO, with the reason, the numbers and a "Fix it" button. One NO-GO holds the launch. A unanimous GO opens the 4-of-4 signature.

5. Launch: a 3D flight that meets a real solar storm from NASA DONKI records of the last 30 days.

6. Operate: run the station, satellite or outpost turn by turn: power, water, data, storms and impacts.

7. Debrief: a score for science, safety, efficiency and collaboration, plain-language lessons on why the mission worked or failed, and a button to publish your design to the network.


Design is a loop, as in real mission engineering: you can go back to any step, add a part, take a partner's open technology or a rideshare deal, and come back to the review. Two ways to play: Guided by Rocky, a mascot who points at the key controls, or Quick play, where every step comes pre-filled with a recommended choice.


THE MOMENTS WE DESIGNED FOR

- A partner says NO-GO and shows you the number that is wrong. You fix it, and you feel why consensus makes missions safer.

- Four keys sign the manifest with the same post-quantum standard NIST approved in 2024, inside a game.

- A solar storm that really happened last week hits your spacecraft, labeled with its NASA record.

- The spare mass on your rocket becomes a seat for a smaller nation's experiment, and your budget grows because you shared.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

- For students: a whole mission, from concept to operations, with the trade-offs engineers really face (mass and power margins, power in shadow, link coverage, launch capacity, budget) and a public source behind every number.

- For classrooms and clubs: up to four players share one screen and argue GO or NO-GO, so systems engineering and teamwork are learned together.

- For the space community: a working prototype of transparent, verifiable governance for multinational missions: shared rules, signed decisions, open designs, and spare rocket capacity that lets smaller nations fly.

- The impact we aim for: classrooms and student CubeSat teams around the world on one open network, where designs and data are shared and every decision can be verified.


HOW IT WORKS

- A React 19 and TypeScript single-page app, served with a small API by one Cloudflare Worker.

- The mission engine is pure, deterministic TypeScript (same inputs and seed, same result), covered by automated tests. It computes the six gauges, flies the mission with seeded random events, and runs Operations turn by turn.

- Risk assessment: the engine flies your design 200 times with different seeds and reports the share that succeed, following NASA probabilistic risk assessment practice (NASA/SP-2011-3421).

- Readiness review: each check compares the engine's numbers with NASA practice, such as a 10% margin on mass, power, link and budget (NASA Goddard GSFC-STD-1000G) and at least 70% simulated success for a clean GO. The review itself is modeled on NASA pre-launch readiness reviews (NPD 8610.24C).

- Signatures: each council member signs a SHA-256 digest of the mission manifest with ed25519 plus ML-DSA-65 (NIST FIPS 204), in the browser, and the game verifies every signature in both schemes.

- Live data: the Worker fetches, caches and cleans the NASA feeds. When a feed is down, the game falls back to a bundled snapshot, so it works offline and with no keys. An in-game "NASA live" panel shows each source and whether it is live.

- Shared, verifiable results: published designs and the leaderboard live in Supabase, and the Worker replays the flight and Operations before a score counts. Nicknames only, no personal data.

- Optional public record: a signed mission can be recorded on the Solana devnet (a public test network) as a memo, the way a DAO records its decisions. Play credits only: test network, no tokens, no real money.


TOOLS

Source code: https://github.com/xdayon/SpaceDAO. React 19, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, zustand and motion for the front end. three.js, React Three Fiber, drei and postprocessing for 3D, with NASA textures. @noble/curves, @noble/post-quantum and @noble/hashes for cryptography. Cloudflare Workers for hosting and the API, Supabase for the design registry and leaderboard, Solana devnet for the optional record. Vitest, ESLint and GitHub Actions on every pull request. Flags from flag-icons; fonts Michroma, Inter and JetBrains Mono. Remotion for the demo video. Open source under Apache 2.0.


WHAT IS CREATIVE

- Governance as gameplay. Real missions depend on who decides, who pays and who flies. SpaceDAO makes that playable: a mission charter, a Go / No-Go review, barter between partners as on the ISS, and a signature from every partner before launch.

- Web3 without the hype. We use the parts of Web3 that help science (shared rules, public records, verifiable signatures, open designs) and leave out the parts that do not (tokens, speculation, wallets).

- Live NASA records as game events. Solar storms, wildfires and volcanoes come from NASA DONKI and EONET records, each labeled with its source.

- Sharing with real trade-offs. An open design costs integration mass or power and asks you to publish your own design back. Spare rocket room earns budget by carrying another team's payload.

- A public source behind every real number, one tap away.

WHAT WE CONSIDERED

- The audience: clear and beautiful within five minutes, understandable to a curious teenager and credible to a mission engineer. Plain language first, numbers and sources one tap below.

- Honesty: no tokens, no money, no wallet, no personal data. The chain record is optional and on a test network.

- Resilience: works with no network and no API keys, using bundled NASA snapshots.

- Respect: no agency logos, insignia or mission patches anywhere. SpaceDAO is not endorsed by NASA or any agency.

- Next steps: open the network to real classrooms and student CubeSat teams, add zero-knowledge proofs so partners can prove a design meets the rules without exposing export-controlled details, and let schools, scientists and the public fund shared payloads together through quadratic funding, so a team in any country can join a mission.


USE OF SUPER INTELLIGENCE (SI) TOOLS

- Audio: the narration voice in our demo videos is SI-generated (ElevenLabs). This is stated here and in each video file's metadata.

- Images: the SpaceDAO logo image on our team page was generated with ChatGPT from our concept and carries a visible "AI-generated" mark. The logo inside the game is drawn in code. All game art is drawn in code (SVG and three.js); the 3D Earth and Moon use NASA public-domain imagery.

- Code and data: we used Anthropic's Claude to research sourced data, write and review code, and draft documentation. A team member reviewed every SI-assisted change. Each SI-assisted commit carries a "Co-Authored-By" line in its metadata, and the README has a "Use of AI" section.

- Not SI-generated: music by Scott Buckley (CC BY 4.0), interface and sci-fi effects by Kenney (CC0), launch sound from NASA engine test audio (public domain). The game itself uses no SI at runtime.

- Source code (Apache 2.0): https://github.com/xdayon/SpaceDAO
